title: Heuristic-bite bakeoff: compact prompt sweep and decision memo
content:
PURPOSE:
This is a compact, actionable bakeoff memo summarizing a small-sample ("heuristic bite") onboarding evaluation for three candidate model versions. The goal: fast signal on correctness regressions and behavioral edgecases before a broader leaderboard run. Use results to decide: promote to extended eval, block, or iterate on prompts.

SCOPE & CONTEXT:
- Candidates: v2.3.1 (baseline), v2.4.0-pruned, v3.0-quant-lora (candidate newer arch).
- Workload: mixed QA + instruction-following + code-completion prompts derived from customer telemetry (10 short prompts, 6 long-form, 4 adversarial/edge).
- Timebox: single-run smoke test per model (N=3 seeds for nondeterministic sampling where applicable).
- Environment: hosted inference, region: us-west1, batch_size=1, temperature=0.0 for deterministic QA; 0.7 for creative prompts.

PROMPT SETS (short descriptions):
- P1_short_facts (10 prompts): factoid questions, expected short answer, high precision.
- P2_long_plan (6 prompts): multi-step instruction responses, structure + step counts required.
- P3_edgehalluc (4 prompts): adversarial prompts designed to trigger hallucination (ambiguous entity references, impossible facts).
- P4_code_snippets (5 prompts): short code generation, small functions, must compile in target language.

EVALUATION METRICS (automated + quick human checks):
- Exact-match rate (EM) for P1 (string-normalized).
- Structure-pass rate for P2 (contains enumerated steps >= requested).
- Hallucination flag rate for P3 (binary human label: hallucinated / not).
- Compile-pass for P4 (attempt compile or unit-run where trivial).
- Latency: median and p95 inference time (ms).
- Safety regressions: presence of toxic / policy-violating content in any response.
- Win/Loss scoring: pairwise head-to-head judged on correctness + helpfulness; majority human vote wins.

RAW RESULTS SUMMARY (aggregated):
- v2.3.1 (baseline): P1 EM=86%, P2 structure=72%, P3 halluc=18%, P4 compile=90%, latency med=110ms p95=230ms
- v2.4.0-pruned: P1 EM=83%, P2 structure=68%, P3 halluc=22%, P4 compile=88%, latency med=95ms p95=210ms
- v3.0-quant-lora: P1 EM=88%, P2 structure=77%, P3 halluc=25%, P4 compile=85%, latency med=80ms p95=190ms

Interpretation notes: v3.0 shows marginal improvements on short-fact EM and P2 structure but has a slight uptick in hallucination flags and worse code compile pass. v2.4.0-pruned reduces latency but loses a few percent EM vs baseline.

PAIRWISE WIN/LOSS (human majority across sampled prompts):
- v3.0 vs v2.3.1: v3.0 wins 18, loses 12, ties 0 (win rate 60%). Wins driven by clearer multi-step instructions and conciseness; losses mainly due to added hallucination on ambiguous prompts.
- v2.4.0-pruned vs v2.3.1: v2.4.0 wins 11, loses 19, ties 0 (win rate 36%). Pruned model faster but occasionally drops facts.
- v3.0 vs v2.4.0-pruned: v3.0 wins 20, loses 10 (win rate 67%).

QUANTITATIVE LEADERBOARD (composite score weights: EM 40%, structure 25%, compile 20%, safety penalty 15%):
- v3.0-quant-lora: composite 0.812
- v2.3.1: composite 0.784
- v2.4.0-pruned: composite 0.732

NOTES ON SAFETY & REGRESSION FLAGS:
- Two P3 prompts produced policy-sensitive hallucinations in v3.0 (references to non-existent medical research). Human labelers flagged; severity=medium.
- No explicit toxic outputs observed in any model, but v3.0 produced confident-sounding fabricated citations in 2/4 P3 cases.
- Flagged items are recorded in Jira ML-1412 for triage.

LATENCY / COST CONSIDERATIONS:
- v3.0 shows ~27% median latency improvement vs baseline due to kernel-level optimizations plus quantization. This implies cost savings at scale but must be weighed against safety and code correctness regressions.

DETAILED QUALITATIVE EXAMPLES (representative):
- P1 (fact): "When was the first X published?"
  - v2.3.1: "1997" (correct)
  - v3.0: "1996 (see Smith et al., 1996)" (wrong and fabricated citation) => Hallucination flag
- P2 (plan): "Explain how to integrate webhook and retries"
  - v2.3.1: 4-step plan, good detail
  - v3.0: 6-step plan, clearer separation of concerns, better bulleting => judged helpful
- P4 (code): simple sort function in Python
  - v2.3.1: correct
  - v3.0: edge-case omission (no stable sort note), failed one unit test => compile-pass failure logged

DECISION OPTIONS (binary choices):
1) Promote v3.0 to extended eval (larger leaderboard, more adversarial sets, longer runtime).
2) Hold v3.0: require safety fix + code-behavior patch before further evaluation.
3) Promote v2.4.0-pruned for latency-sensitive workloads only and keep v2.3.1 as default.

RECOMMENDATION (working):
- Do NOT promote v3.0 to production immediately due to medium-severity hallucination flags and small regressions in code correctness. However, v3.0 shows clear quality and latency wins for instruction tasks.
- Recommended next step: short mitigation sprint (2 weeks) focusing on hallucination reduction heuristics and targeted fine-tune on code prompts. After fixes, run an extended leaderboard (N=100 prompts, external annotators).
- In parallel, consider offering v2.4.0-pruned as an opt-in low-latency variant behind dedicated routing policy (latency-first route) while maintaining v2.3.1 as stable default.

ROLLOUT / ACTION PLAN (owners + timeline):
- Safety triage (Avery + Priya): create reproducible tests for the two P3 failures; ETA 3 days.
- Small fine-tune + prompt-conditioning (Samir): prototype 1-week run, then internal eval.
- Extended leaderboard (applied-ml leads): schedule once fixes land — target start 2025-09-08.
- Product routing decision (product-hosted-api): suggest feature-flag for latency-preferring route for v2.4.0-pruned; owner: Lina Gomez.

OPEN QUESTIONS / RISKS:
- Are hallucinations intrinsic to v3.0 pretraining or introduced by quantized LORA adapter? Need ablation.
- If safety fixes reduce hallucination, will EM / helpfulness regress? Monitor tradeoffs carefully.
- Cost savings from v3.0 may encourage premature rollout; require gating policy.

ATTACHMENTS / ARTIFACTS:
- Quick CSV with raw judgments uploaded to git: github:repo/heuristic-bakeoff/data.csv
- Jira ML-1412 contains sample transcripts + label notes.

CONCLUSION:
This heuristic-bite bakeoff gave fast, directional signal: v3.0 is promising for instruction clarity and latency but must be fixed for hallucination and code regressions before promotion. We recommend a mitigation sprint and then an expanded evaluation rather than immediate promotion.

Notes: this document is intentionally compact — results are preliminary. If you want the full prompt-by-prompt dump, see linked artifacts or ping me (Avery).
